---
title: "Telematics CANN — Claim Count Modelling"
output: html_notebook

Reproduction of the cross-sectional models of Duval, Boucher & Pigeon (2024), fit on
the public So, Boucher & Valdez (2021) synthetic telematics portfolio. See `README.md`
for the paper background and scope decisions (MVNB is out of scope: this data is
cross-sectional, one row per policy, no insured id).

# 0. Setup

```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table)   # data wrangling
  library(dplyr)         # a few readable verbs (case_when, mutate)
  library(ggplot2)       # plotting
  library(ggcorrplot)    # correlation heatmap
  library(MASS)           # glm.nb
  library(splines)        # ns()
  library(AER)             # dispersiontest (Cameron-Trivedi)
  library(pscl)            # pR2
  library(car)             # vif
  library(glmnet)          # kept for reference; not used in the final variable-selection path
  # library(torch)  
  library(keras3)# CANN
})
```

# 1. Data load and cleaning

```{r load}
dt <- fread("telematics_syn-032021.csv") # faster than read_csv and handles separators directly 
cat("dim:", dim(dt), "\n")
```

```{r structural-checks}
stopifnot(nrow(dt) == 100000, ncol(dt) == 52)
cat("missing values:", sum(is.na(dt)), " | duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(dt)), "\n")
table(dt$Insured.sex, dt$Marital)
table(dt$Car.use, dt$Region)
```

- No missing values. `Insured.sex` (Male/Female), `Region` (Urban/Rural) are binary.
  `Car.use` has 4 levels (Commercial, Commute, Farmer, Private), two of which carry
  very little exposure — handled in §4.
- `Territory` has ~55 levels with no obvious hierarchy to bin it by; per the project's
  scope, it's dropped rather than one-hot-encoded into a GLM.

```{r drop-territory}
cat("Territory levels:", uniqueN(dt$Territory), "\n")
dt[, Territory := NULL]
summary(dt)
```

`Car.age` has negative values (model year ahead of the policy year — a data error,
not a real "negative age"). **Correction to the original pass at this notebook:**

```{r fix-car-age}
n_bad_age <- dt[Car.age < 0, .N]
cat("negative Car.age rows:", n_bad_age, "\n")
med_car_age <- median(dt[Car.age >= 0, Car.age])
dt[Car.age < 0, Car.age := med_car_age]
```

```{r exposure-response}
dt[, Exposure := Duration / 365]  # Duration is in DAYS, so cobveret to years 
summary(dt$Exposure)

table(dt$NB_Claim)
cat(sprintf("policies with >=1 claim: %d (%.2f%%)\n", dt[NB_Claim > 0, .N], 100 * dt[NB_Claim > 0, .N] / nrow(dt)))
cat("portfolio frequency:", dt[, sum(NB_Claim) / sum(Exposure)], "\n")
```

No contract has more than 3 claims; ~4.3% of policies have at least one claim.

Two columns have spaces in their names, which is friction for everything downstream —
rename once, up front:

```{r rename-cols}
setnames(dt, c("Pct.drive.rush am", "Pct.drive.rush pm"),
             c("Pct.drive.rush.am", "Pct.drive.rush.pm"))
```

# 2. Split, then a robust method for continuous-variable form selection

## 2.1 60 / 20 / 20 split, stratified on whether a claim occurred

The dataset is cross-sectional (one row per policy), so a simple random split is
valid — there's no vehicle/insured grouping constraint to respect. Stratifying on
`HasClaim` keeps the ~4.3% positive rate stable across all three sets. 

```{r split}
dt[, HasClaim := as.integer(NB_Claim > 0)]

stratified_split <- function(n_idx, strata, p_train = 0.6, p_valid = 0.2, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  parts <- lapply(split(n_idx, strata), function(idx) {
    idx <- sample(idx); n <- length(idx)
    n_tr <- floor(p_train * n); n_va <- floor(p_valid * n)
    list(train = idx[seq_len(n_tr)],
         valid = idx[n_tr + seq_len(n_va)],
         test  = idx[(n_tr + n_va + 1):n])
  })
  list(train = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "train"), use.names = FALSE),
       valid = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "valid"), use.names = FALSE),
       test  = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "test"),  use.names = FALSE))
}

sp <- stratified_split(seq_len(nrow(dt)), dt$HasClaim)
train <- dt[sp$train]; valid <- dt[sp$valid]; test <- dt[sp$test]
cat("rows:", nrow(train), nrow(valid), nrow(test), "\n")
cat("claim rate by split:", mean(train$HasClaim), mean(valid$HasClaim), mean(test$HasClaim), "\n")
```

## 2.2 The linear-vs-spline-vs-bands decision, made the same way for every variable

For the continuous variables like credit score or age , we have to decide , if we will consider the relationship to be linear, non linear or by bands. But before , i want to look at the exposure and frequency for those variables 
```{r}
continuous_vars <- c("Insured.age", "Car.age", "Credit.score", "Years.noclaims", "Annual.miles.drive")
#plotting dunction
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

freq_cont_plot <- function(dt,var,exposure = "Exposure",target = "NB_Claim", n_bands = 10) {

  tmp <- copy(dt)
  breaks = unique (quantile(dt[[var]], probs = seq(0,1, length.out= n_bands+1), na.rm=TRUE))

  tmp[, Band := cut(
    get(var),breaks = breaks, inclue.lowest = TRUE) ]

  res <- tmp[
    ,
    .(
      Exposure = sum(get(exposure), na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims = sum(get(target), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    by = Band
  ]

  res[, Frequency := Claims / Exposure]

  scale_factor <- max(res$Exposure) /
                  max(res$Frequency)

  p <- ggplot(res, aes(x = Band)) +
    geom_col(
      aes(y = Exposure),
      fill = "lightblue",
      alpha = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_line(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor, group = 1),
      color = "red",
      linewidth = 1.2
    ) +
    geom_point(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor),
      color = "red",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Exposure",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        ~ . / scale_factor,
        name = "Claim Frequency"
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Exposure and Claim Frequency by", var),
      x = var
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(
        angle = 45,
        hjust = 1
      )
    )

  print(p)

  invisible(res)
}

for (v in continuous_vars) {
  freq_cont_plot(dt, v)
}
```
Before doing any tghing else, how is the claim frequency distributed ? poisson ? or negative binomial ? 
```{r}
cat("the mean of the nb_claim is :", mean(dt$NB_Claim), "the variance is", var(dt$NB_Claim) )
# variance is higher so we choose negative binomiale as distribution for nb_claim

```


In doing my model, i need to decide how to represent the continuous variables rlationships with the frequency 
wether considering a linear relationship but by bands or a non linear one 
represented byba spline.and keep the
simplest form that isn't measurably worse than the best one.

```{r form-selection-fn}
poisson_deviance <- function(y, pred) 2 * sum(ifelse(y == 0, pred, y * log(y / pred) - (y - pred)))

choose_var_form_dev <- function(var, train, valid, target = "NB_Claim", exposure = "Exposure",
                             nbands = 6, df_spline = 4) {
  br <- unique(quantile(train[[var]], probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = nbands + 1), na.rm = TRUE))
  br[1] <- -Inf; br[length(br)] <- Inf

  tr <- copy(train); va <- copy(valid)
  tr[, band := cut(get(var), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]
  va[, band := cut(get(var), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]

  f_lin    <- reformulate(c(var, sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)
  f_spline <- reformulate(c(sprintf("splines::ns(%s, df = %d)", var, df_spline),
                             sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)
  f_band   <- reformulate(c("band", sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)

  m_lin <- glm(f_lin, data = tr, family = poisson())
  m_spl <- glm(f_spline, data = tr, family = poisson())
  m_bnd <- glm(f_band, data = tr, family = poisson())

  data.table(
    variable = var, form = c("linear", "spline_df4", "bands"),
    n_params = c(1, df_spline, nlevels(tr$band) - 1),
    valid_deviance = c(
      poisson_deviance(va[[target]], predict(m_lin, va, type = "response")),
      poisson_deviance(va[[target]], predict(m_spl, va, type = "response")),
      poisson_deviance(va[[target]], predict(m_bnd, va, type = "response"))
    )
  )
}
```


now same but for negative binomial log likelihood 
```{r}
neg_log_like <- function(y, mu, theta) -sum(dnbinom(x=y, mu=mu, size = theta, log=TRUE))

choose_var_form_neg <- function(var, train, valid, target = "NB_Claim", exposure = "Exposure",
                             nbands = 6, df_spline = 4) {
  br <- unique(quantile(train[[var]], probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = nbands + 1), na.rm = TRUE))
  br[1] <- -Inf; br[length(br)] <- Inf

  tr <- copy(train); va <- copy(valid)
  tr[, band := cut(get(var), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]
  va[, band := cut(get(var), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]

  f_lin    <- reformulate(c(var, sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)
  f_spline <- reformulate(c(sprintf("splines::ns(%s, df = %d)", var, df_spline),
                             sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)
  f_band   <- reformulate(c("band", sprintf("offset(log(%s))", exposure)), response = target)

  m_lin <- MASS :: glm.nb(f_lin, data = tr)
  m_spl <- glm.nb(f_spline, data = tr)
  m_bnd <- glm.nb(f_band, data = tr)

  data.table(
    variable = var, form = c("linear", "spline_df4", "bands"),
    n_params = c(1, df_spline, nlevels(tr$band) - 1),
    valid_nb_ll = c(
      neg_log_like(va[[target]], predict(m_lin, va, type = "response"), m_lin$theta),
      neg_log_like(va[[target]], predict(m_spl, va, type = "response"), m_spl$theta),
      neg_log_like(va[[target]], predict(m_bnd, va, type = "response"), m_bnd$theta)
    )
  )
}
```

now we choose the most appropriate form to represnete each continous variable based
on the poisson deviance and negative log likelihood(since negative , the lower the better )
```{r form-selection-run poisson deviance }
form_results <- rbindlist(lapply(continuous_vars, choose_var_form_dev, train = train, valid = valid))
print(form_results)

## Decision rule: among forms within 0.05% of the best validation deviance for that
## variable, keep the one with the fewest parameters (ties: linear < spline < bands)
form_order <- c(linear = 1, spline_df4 = 2, bands = 3)
decision <- form_results[
  , .SD[valid_deviance <= min(valid_deviance) * 1.0005][order(n_params, form_order[form])][1],
  by = variable
]
cat("\nchosen forms:\n")
print(decision[, .(variable, form, n_params, valid_deviance)])
```

```{r form-selection-run negative_log_likelihood }
form_results2 <- rbindlist(lapply(continuous_vars, choose_var_form_neg, train = train, valid = valid))
print(form_results2)

## Decision rule: among forms within 0.05% of the best validation deviance for that
## variable, keep the one with the fewest parameters (ties: linear < spline < bands)
form_order <- c(linear = 1, spline_df4 = 2, bands = 3)
decision2 <- form_results2[
  , .SD[valid_nb_ll <= min(valid_nb_ll) * 1.0005][order(n_params, form_order[form])][1],
  by = variable
]
cat("\nchosen forms:\n")
print(decision2[, .(variable, form, n_params, valid_nb_ll)])
```

Both poisson deviance and negative binomial log likelihood agree that 
Everything wants a spline except `Car.age`, which the *out-of-sample* deviance says
is adequately linear. That's a useful result in itself: an in-sample, one-way-plot
read of `Car.age` can look like it has a non-monotone "shoulder", but that shape
doesn't survive a held-out check — a small illustration of exactly why this method
(validated out of sample, not eyeballed) is the more defensible one to use uniformly.

```{r form-selection-materialise}
## materialise the chosen form as a model term, 
make_term <- function(v, df_spline = 4, nbands = 6) {
  frm <- decision2[variable == v, form]
  if (frm == "linear") return(v)
  if (frm == "spline_df4") return(sprintf("splines::ns(%s, df = %d)", v, df_spline))
  br <- unique(quantile(train[[v]], probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = nbands + 1), na.rm = TRUE))
  br[1] <- -Inf; br[length(br)] <- Inf
  bandcol <- paste0(v, ".band")
  train[, (bandcol) := cut(get(v), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]
  valid[, (bandcol) := cut(get(v), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]
  test[,  (bandcol) := cut(get(v), breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE)]
  bandcol
}
continuous_terms <- setNames(sapply(continuous_vars, make_term), continuous_vars)
print(continuous_terms)
```

# 3. Categorical variables and telematics collinearity

## 3.1 Categorical variables
a look at the exposure and frequency by caetgorical variables int he 

```{r cat-freq}
categorical_vars <- c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use")
freq_by_cat <- function(v, data = dt) {
  data[, .(Exposure = sum(Exposure), Claims = sum(NB_Claim)), by = v][
    , Frequency := Claims / Exposure][order(-Exposure)]
}
for (v in categorical_vars) { cat("\n--", v, "--\n"); print(freq_by_cat(v)) }
```
- we are more exposed to male policyholders, we have more claims for males, 
yet less frequency, so everything else held constant , malke have less frequencies 

- we have about twice the exposure to married people, and they have lower frequencies ceteris paribus 

- We have about 4 times the exposure to Urban regions, and they have higher frequencies ceteris parisbus 

- Farmers have the lowest frequency, and commute have the highest frequency, 
but we have too low exposure to commercial and farmer which may affect our models performance and prudence 
we will merge those two into the bigger level rhqt is Commute 

```{r car-use-merge}
cu <- freq_by_cat("Car.use")
big   <- cu[Exposure %in% sort(Exposure, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2], Car.use]
small <- setdiff(cu$Car.use, big)
map <- sapply(small, function(s) {
  f_s <- cu[Car.use == s, Frequency]
  big[which.min(abs(cu[Car.use %in% big, Frequency] - f_s))]
})
print(map)

apply_car_use_grp <- function(d) {
  d[, Car.use.grp := Car.use]
  for (s in names(map)) d[Car.use.grp == s, Car.use.grp := map[[s]]]
  d[, Car.use.grp := factor(Car.use.grp)]
}
apply_car_use_grp(train); apply_car_use_grp(valid); apply_car_use_grp(test)
table(train$Car.use, train$Car.use.grp)
```

```{r cat-plot}
categorical_vars <- c(categorical_vars, "Car.use.grp")
for (v in categorical_vars) print(
  ggplot(freq_by_cat(v, data = train), aes(reorder(get(v), Frequency), Frequency)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + coord_flip() +
    labs(title = paste("Observed frequency by", v), x = NULL) + theme_minimal()
)
```
convert the categorical variables to factors in the datasets 
```{r cat-to-factor}
to_factor <- function(d, v, lev) d[, (v) := factor(get(v), levels = lev)]
for (v in c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region")) { # Car.use.grp is already a factor
  lev <- sort(unique(train[[v]]))
  to_factor(train, v, lev); to_factor(valid, v, lev); to_factor(test, v, lev)
}
```

## 3.2 Telematics collinearity, and a data-driven GLM-B shortlist

The harsh-event and turn-intensity families are nested threshold counts (the 06mph
threshold count is always ≥ the 14mph count), so they're collinear by construction;
the day-of-week percentages are compositional. This is exactly why the CANN routes
telematics through the MLP rather than the log-linear part: a GLM needs one
de-correlated representative per family, a network can absorb the redundant block.

```{r telematics-corr}
telematics_all <- c(
  "Annual.pct.driven", "Total.miles.driven", "Avgdays.week",
  "Pct.drive.mon","Pct.drive.tue","Pct.drive.wed","Pct.drive.thr","Pct.drive.fri","Pct.drive.sat","Pct.drive.sun",
  "Pct.drive.wkday","Pct.drive.wkend",
  "Pct.drive.2hrs","Pct.drive.3hrs","Pct.drive.4hrs","Pct.drive.rush.am","Pct.drive.rush.pm",
  "Accel.06miles","Accel.08miles","Accel.09miles","Accel.11miles","Accel.12miles","Accel.14miles",
  "Brake.06miles","Brake.08miles","Brake.09miles","Brake.11miles","Brake.12miles","Brake.14miles",
  "Left.turn.intensity08","Left.turn.intensity09","Left.turn.intensity10","Left.turn.intensity11","Left.turn.intensity12",
  "Right.turn.intensity08","Right.turn.intensity09","Right.turn.intensity10","Right.turn.intensity11","Right.turn.intensity12"
)
corr <- cor(train[, ..telematics_all], use = "complete.obs")
ggcorrplot(corr, type = "lower", colors = c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")) +
  ggtitle("Telematics correlation matrix") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))

high_pairs <- which(abs(corr) > 0.9 & upper.tri(corr), arr.ind = TRUE)
pairs_dt <- data.table(var1 = rownames(corr)[high_pairs[,1]], var2 = colnames(corr)[high_pairs[,2]],
                        r = corr[high_pairs])[order(-abs(r))]
cat("highly correlated pairs (|r|>0.9):", nrow(pairs_dt), "\n")
head(pairs_dt, 10)
```

For the GLM-B benchmark (I will choose one variable by covariate family 
univariate AIC against the target, so the choice is data-driven rather than an
arbitrary pick of the harshest threshold:

```{r telematics-shortlist}
# calcule aics for a group of variables and returns the set that return the lowest AIC 
# then we will pick the best per family of telemeatrics data 
family_best <- function(vars) {
  aics <- sapply(vars, function(v) {
    f <- reformulate(c(v, "offset(log(Exposure))"), response = "NB_Claim")
    # AIC(glm(f, data = train, family = poisson()))
    AIC(glm.nb(f, data = train)) # using NB distribution
  })
  names(which.min(aics))
}
accel_best <- family_best(c("Accel.06miles","Accel.08miles","Accel.09miles","Accel.11miles","Accel.12miles","Accel.14miles"))
brake_best <- family_best(c("Brake.06miles","Brake.08miles","Brake.09miles","Brake.11miles","Brake.12miles","Brake.14miles"))
lturn_best <- family_best(c("Left.turn.intensity08","Left.turn.intensity09","Left.turn.intensity10","Left.turn.intensity11","Left.turn.intensity12"))
rturn_best <- family_best(c("Right.turn.intensity08","Right.turn.intensity09","Right.turn.intensity10",
                            "Right.turn.intensity11","Right.turn.intensity12"))

## keep brake_best / lturn_best; accel_best and rturn_best are near-duplicates of them
telematics_glmB <- c("Total.miles.driven", "Avgdays.week", "Pct.drive.wkend",
                     "Pct.drive.rush.am", "Pct.drive.rush.pm", brake_best, lturn_best)
telematics_glmB
```

# 4. GLM-A / GLM-B benchmarks and dispersion diagnostics

## 4.1 GLM-A (traditional only) and GLM-B (traditional + hand-picked telematics)

```{r glmA-glmB}
# model A uses only the policy data 
rhs_trad <- c(unname(continuous_terms), "Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use.grp")
f_glmA <- reformulate(c(rhs_trad, "offset(log(Exposure))"), response = "NB_Claim")
glmA_pois <- glm(f_glmA, data = train, family = poisson())
# hte second model uses + telematric best family data 
rhs_full <- c(rhs_trad, telematics_glmB)
f_glmB <- reformulate(c(rhs_full, "offset(log(Exposure))"), response = "NB_Claim")
glmB_pois_full <- glm(f_glmB, data = train, family = poisson())

car::vif(glmB_pois_full)
```
VIFs (per-df adjusted, `GVIF^(1/(2*Df))`) are all comfortably under 1.5 — the
family-representative screen already resolved the collinearity that mattered.

testing the significativity of all bvariables in the full glmB model 

```{r glmB-prune}
d1 <- drop1(glmB_pois_full, test = "Chisq")
print(d1)
# dropping the ones that are not statistically significants 
drop_terms <- rownames(d1)[which(d1$`Pr(>Chi)` > 0.05)]
drop_terms
# the variables Insured.sex; Marital ; Car.use.grep ; Avg.day.wk ; are bnot statiscticaly significants so we 
# drop them then update the glmB 
f_glmB <- update(f_glmB, paste(". ~ . -", paste(drop_terms, collapse = " - "))) 
glmB_pois <- glm(f_glmB, data = train, family = poisson())
f_glmB
```

```{r glmA-glmB-validate}
# fnc that calculate the poisson deviance training / validation dataset 
val_dev <- function(m, newdata) poisson_deviance(newdata$NB_Claim, predict(m, newdata, type = "response"))

cat(sprintf("validation Poisson deviance -- GLM-A: %.1f | GLM-B: %.1f\n", val_dev(glmA_pois, valid), val_dev(glmB_pois, valid)))
```
GLM-B has a far lower deviance on validation set and 
materially beats GLM-A out of sample — telematics carry real signal even
through a hand-picked, log-linear lens.

## 4.2 Dispersion diagnostics: does this portfolio need Negative Binomial?

Decision sequence: marginal ratio (crude) → Cameron-Trivedi score test → **Pearson
dispersion after fitting the Poisson GLM** (the one that actually decides it, since
covariates may absorb marginal heterogeneity) → LR test vs NB (boundary mixture, so
the usual p-value is halved).

```{r dispersion}
y <- train$NB_Claim
cat("marginal var/mean ratio:", var(y) / mean(y), "\n")

cat("\nCameron-Trivedi score test, GLM-A (traditional only):\n")
print(AER::dispersiontest(glmA_pois, trafo = 1))

phi <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
cat("\nPearson dispersion phi -- GLM-A:", phi(glmA_pois), "| GLM-B:", phi(glmB_pois), "\n")
```

Pearson φ is close to 1 for GLM-A (covariates absorb most of the marginal
overdispersion), but the Cameron-Trivedi score test and the LR test below are still
significant — a useful nuance: φ≈1 alone would have been misleading here, the formal
tests are what actually settle it.

```{r dispersion-nb}
glmA_nb <- glm.nb(f_glmA, data = train)
glmB_nb <- glm.nb(f_glmB, data = train)

alpha_A <- 1 / glmA_nb$theta; alpha_B <- 1 / glmB_nb$theta
cat(sprintf("NB dispersion alpha_hat -- traditional only: %.4f | + telematics: %.4f (%.1f%% shrinkage)\n",
            alpha_A, alpha_B, 100 * (alpha_A - alpha_B) / alpha_A))

lr_stat <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(glmA_nb)) - as.numeric(logLik(glmA_pois)))
lr_p <- 0.5 * pchisq(lr_stat, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("LR test Poisson vs NB (traditional only): stat=%.1f, p=%.2e\n", lr_stat, lr_p))
```

**This is the single most persuasive result available from the GLM side**: the NB
dispersion parameter shrinks substantially once telematics are added. In the
Poisson-Gamma mixture interpretation, α̂ measures unobserved heterogeneity ("frailty")
the rating factors don't capture — and telematics explain part of it. NB is used from
here on as the primary distributional family, per the LR test above.

The telematics information captures latent risk characteristics and significantly 
reduces unobserved heterogeneity within the portfolio.

and since : the p- value is less than 5% I strongly reject the Poisson assumption.
There is highly significant evidence of overdispersion in the claim counts. 
The Poisson model understates the variability observed in the data, 
and the Negative Binomial model provides a statistically superior fit.

# 5. The CANN

## 5.1 Architecture, of the model 

```
log(mu_i) = log(exposure_i)          <- offset of exposure
          + x_i^trad . beta          <- log-linear ("actuarial") part: TRADITIONAL factors only
          + MLP(x_i^trad, x_i^tele)  <- network part: traditional AND telematics
```
The log-linear part is deliberately restricted to traditional factors — it's the
stable, interpretable backbone, and it's exactly GLM-A's formula (`f_glmA`) so the
warm start below is well-defined. The MLP receives traditional factors (raw, not
splined — the network can shape its own non-linearities) **and all ~38 telematics
columns**, unfiltered by any hand-picked shortlist, so it can learn interactions a
hand-engineered feature set structurally cannot.

**Warm start**: β is initialised at GLM-A's fitted coefficients, and the MLP's output
layer is initialised at zero. At epoch 0 the CANN is numerically identical to GLM-A;
gradient descent can only move away from it in directions that improve the
likelihood.

```{r cann-design-matrices}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(torch))

mm <- function(formula, data) model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula)), data)

X_trad_train <- mm(f_glmA, train); X_trad_valid <- mm(f_glmA, valid); X_trad_test <- mm(f_glmA, test)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(X_trad_train), names(coef(glmA_pois))))

trad_numeric <- c("Insured.age", "Car.age", "Credit.score", "Years.noclaims", "Annual.miles.drive")
trad_dummies <- c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use.grp")

std_from_train <- function(x) list(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
num_stats  <- lapply(train[, ..trad_numeric], std_from_train)
tele_stats <- lapply(train[, ..telematics_all], std_from_train)

scale_block <- function(data, vars, stats) {
  m <- sapply(vars, function(v) (data[[v]] - stats[[v]]$mean) / stats[[v]]$sd)
  colnames(m) <- vars; m
}
mlp_input <- function(data) cbind(
  scale_block(data, trad_numeric, num_stats),
  model.matrix(~ . - 1, data[, ..trad_dummies]),
  scale_block(data, telematics_all, tele_stats)
)
X_mlp_train <- mlp_input(train); 
X_mlp_valid <- mlp_input(valid); 
X_mlp_test <- mlp_input(test)

offset_train <- log(train$Exposure); offset_valid <- log(valid$Exposure); offset_test <- log(test$Exposure)

y_train <- train$NB_Claim; y_valid <- valid$NB_Claim; y_test <- test$NB_Claim
beta_glm <- coef(glmA_pois)
cat("X_trad:", dim(X_trad_train), " | X_mlp:", dim(X_mlp_train), "\n")
```

## 5.2 Model definition

`r` (the NB dispersion) is **not** an output of the forward pass — it's a single
global trainable scalar, parameterised on the log scale so it stays positive under
unconstrained gradient descent, updated by the same Adam step as every weight.

```{r cann-module}
cann_module <- nn_module(
  "CANN",
  initialize = function(n_trad, n_mlp, beta_glm, dropout = 0.1) {
    self$lin <- nn_linear(n_trad, 1)
    with_no_grad({
      self$lin$weight$copy_(torch_tensor(matrix(beta_glm[-1], nrow = 1)))
      self$lin$bias$copy_(torch_tensor(beta_glm[1]))
    })
    self$fc1 <- nn_linear(n_mlp, 64)
    self$fc2 <- nn_linear(64, 32)
    self$fc3 <- nn_linear(32, 16)
    self$out <- nn_linear(16, 1)
    with_no_grad({ self$out$weight$zero_(); self$out$bias$zero_() })
    self$drop <- nn_dropout(dropout)
    self$log_r <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(0.0))
  },
  forward = function(x_trad, x_mlp, offset) {
    lin_part <- self$lin(x_trad)
    h <- torch_tanh(self$fc1(x_mlp)); h <- self$drop(h)
    h <- torch_tanh(self$fc2(h))
    h <- torch_tanh(self$fc3(h))
    nn_part <- self$out(h)
    ## offset is a 1-D (batch) tensor; lin_part/nn_part are (batch, 1). Reshape
    ## offset to (batch, 1) before adding -- otherwise `offset + lin_part` silently
    ## broadcasts to a (batch, batch) matrix instead of a per-row sum.
    eta <- offset$unsqueeze(2) + lin_part + nn_part
    eta <- torch_clamp(eta, -12, 6)
    eta$squeeze(2)
  }
)

poisson_nll <- function(eta, y) { mu <- torch_exp(eta); torch_mean(mu - y * torch_log(mu)) }
nb_nll <- function(eta, y, log_r) {
  mu <- torch_exp(eta); r <- torch_exp(log_r)
  ll <- torch_lgamma(y + r) - torch_lgamma(r) - torch_lgamma(y + 1) +
        r * torch_log(r / (r + mu)) + y * torch_log(mu / (r + mu))
  -torch_mean(ll)
}
```

## 5.3 Training loop (mini-batch Adam, early stopping, gradient clipping)

```{r cann-fit-fn}
fit_cann <- function(head = c("poisson", "nb"), seed = 1, epochs = 100, patience = 10,
                      lr = 1e-3, batch_size = 1024, verbose = FALSE) {
  head <- match.arg(head)
 # torch_manual_seed(seed); 
  set.seed(seed)

  net <- cann_module(ncol(X_trad_train) - 1, ncol(X_mlp_train), beta_glm)#network buid
  opt <- optim_adam(net$parameters, lr = lr)
# training tensors : are matrices 
  Xt_tr <- torch_tensor(X_trad_train[, -1, drop = FALSE], dtype = torch_float())
  Xm_tr <- torch_tensor(X_mlp_train, dtype = torch_float())
  y_tr  <- torch_tensor(y_train, dtype = torch_float())
  off_tr <- torch_tensor(offset_train, dtype = torch_float()) # ecxposure offset 
# validation tensors 
  Xt_va <- torch_tensor(X_trad_valid[, -1, drop = FALSE], dtype = torch_float())
  Xm_va <- torch_tensor(X_mlp_valid, dtype = torch_float())
  y_va  <- torch_tensor(y_valid, dtype = torch_float())
  off_va <- torch_tensor(offset_valid, dtype = torch_float()) # exposure log offset 

  n <- nrow(X_trad_train); best_val <- Inf; best_state <- NULL; bad_epochs <- 0
  for (epoch in seq_len(epochs)) {
    net$train()
    idx <- sample.int(n)
    for (b in split(idx, ceiling(seq_along(idx) / batch_size))) {
      opt$zero_grad()
      eta <- net(Xt_tr[b, ], Xm_tr[b, ], off_tr[b])
      loss <- if (head == "poisson") poisson_nll(eta, y_tr[b]) else nb_nll(eta, y_tr[b], net$log_r)
      loss$backward()
      nn_utils_clip_grad_norm_(net$parameters, max_norm = 5)
      opt$step()
    }
    net$eval()
    with_no_grad({
      eta_va <- net(Xt_va, Xm_va, off_va)
      val_loss <- if (head == "poisson") poisson_nll(eta_va, y_va) else nb_nll(eta_va, y_va, net$log_r)
    })
    val_loss <- as.numeric(val_loss)
    if (verbose) cat(sprintf("  epoch %d  val_nll=%.4f\n", epoch, val_loss))
    if (val_loss < best_val - 1e-5) {
      best_val <- val_loss; bad_epochs <- 0
      best_state <- lapply(net$state_dict(), function(t) t$clone())
    } else {
      bad_epochs <- bad_epochs + 1
      if (bad_epochs >= patience) break
    }
  }
  net$load_state_dict(best_state); net$eval()
  list(net = net, best_val_nll = best_val, head = head, seed = seed, epochs_run = epoch)
}
# now preditions of 

predict_cann <- function(fit, X_trad, X_mlp, offset) {
  net <- fit$net; net$eval()
  with_no_grad({
    eta <- net(torch_tensor(X_trad[, -1, drop = FALSE], dtype = torch_float()),
               torch_tensor(X_mlp, dtype = torch_float()),
               torch_tensor(offset, dtype = torch_float()))
  })
  # the return are floats so convert to integer
  as.numeric(torch_exp(eta))
}
```

## 5.4 Multi-seed training: both heads, 5 seeds each

A single-seed improvement over the GLM isn't evidence. Train each head under 5 seeds
and keep every fitted net (needed for the interpretation section) plus its
predictions on all three splits.

```{r cann-train-all}
seeds <- 1:5
cann_fits <- list()
for (head in c("poisson", "nb")) {
  for (s in seeds) {
    key <- paste0(head, "_seed", s)
    fit <- fit_cann(head, seed = s, epochs = 100, patience = 10)
    cann_fits[[key]] <- list(
      fit = fit,
      mu_train = predict_cann(fit, X_trad_train, X_mlp_train, offset_train),
      mu_valid = predict_cann(fit, X_trad_valid, X_mlp_valid, offset_valid),
      mu_test  = predict_cann(fit, X_trad_test,  X_mlp_test,  offset_test),
      log_r = as.numeric(fit$net$log_r)
    )
    cat(sprintf("%s: epochs=%d best_val_nll=%.4f test_deviance=%.1f\n",
                key, fit$epochs_run, fit$best_val_nll,
                poisson_deviance(y_test, cann_fits[[key]]$mu_test)))
  }
}
```

```{r cann-stability}
stability <- rbindlist(lapply(c("poisson", "nb"), function(h) {
  keys <- grep(paste0("^", h, "_seed"), names(cann_fits), value = TRUE)
  devs <- sapply(keys, function(k) poisson_deviance(y_test, cann_fits[[k]]$mu_test))
  data.table(Head = h, mean_test_deviance = mean(devs), sd_test_deviance = sd(devs), n_seeds = length(devs))
}))
print(stability)
```

# 6. Evaluation

Rare-event count problem: accuracy and R² would be meaningless here. Poisson deviance
is the primary, family-comparable ranking metric; NLL is reported but is **not**
comparable between the Poisson and NB models (they're likelihoods of different
distributions).

```{r eval-setup}
own_nll <- function(mu, y, family = c("poisson", "nb"), theta = NULL) {
  family <- match.arg(family)
  if (family == "poisson") -sum(dpois(y, lambda = mu, log = TRUE))
  else -sum(dnbinom(y, mu = mu, size = theta, log = TRUE))
}
eval_row <- function(name, mu, y, family, theta = NULL) {
  data.table(Model = name, Deviance = poisson_deviance(y, mu), Balance = sum(mu) / sum(y),
             OwnNLL = own_nll(mu, y, family, theta))
}
cann_mu <- function(head, split) {
  keys <- grep(paste0("^", head, "_seed"), names(cann_fits), value = TRUE)
  rowMeans(sapply(keys, function(k) cann_fits[[k]][[paste0("mu_", split)]]))
}
cann_theta_nb <- 1 / mean(sapply(grep("^nb_seed", names(cann_fits), value = TRUE),
                                  function(k) exp(cann_fits[[k]]$log_r)))
```

```{r eval-table}
mu_test_list <- list(
  "GLM-A Poisson" = list(mu = predict(glmA_pois, test, type = "response"), family = "poisson"),
  "GLM-A NB"      = list(mu = predict(glmA_nb,   test, type = "response"), family = "nb", theta = glmA_nb$theta),
  "GLM-B Poisson" = list(mu = predict(glmB_pois, test, type = "response"), family = "poisson"),
  "GLM-B NB"      = list(mu = predict(glmB_nb,   test, type = "response"), family = "nb", theta = glmB_nb$theta),
  "CANN-Poisson"  = list(mu = cann_mu("poisson", "test"), family = "poisson"),
  "CANN-NB"       = list(mu = cann_mu("nb", "test"), family = "nb", theta = cann_theta_nb)
)
eval_table <- rbindlist(lapply(names(mu_test_list), function(nm) {
  m <- mu_test_list[[nm]]; eval_row(nm, m$mu, test$NB_Claim, m$family, m$theta)
}))
setorder(eval_table, Deviance)
print(eval_table)
```

**Headline test**: `CANN-NB` vs `GLM-B NB` on Poisson deviance — does a learned
telematics representation beat hand-engineered features?

## 6.1 Gini (ordered Lorenz curve)

Sort policies by predicted risk (`mu/exposure`) ascending; plot cumulative % of
claims against cumulative % of exposure. A model with real discrimination
concentrates claims among the highest-predicted-risk policies, so the curve bows
below the diagonal — Gini = 1 − 2×AUC of that curve.

```{r eval-gini}
ordered_gini <- function(mu, y, exposure) {
  ord <- order(mu / exposure)
  cx <- cumsum(exposure[ord]) / sum(exposure)
  cy <- cumsum(y[ord]) / sum(y)
  auc <- sum(diff(cx) * (head(cy, -1) + tail(cy, -1)) / 2)
  1 - 2 * auc
}
gini_table <- data.table(Model = names(mu_test_list),
                          Gini = sapply(mu_test_list, function(m) ordered_gini(m$mu, test$NB_Claim, test$Exposure)))
setorder(gini_table, -Gini)
print(gini_table)
```

## 6.2 Lift / decile table and calibration

```{r eval-lift}
decile_table <- function(mu, y, exposure, n_bins = 10) {
  ord <- order(mu / exposure)
  bin <- cut(cumsum(exposure[ord]) / sum(exposure), breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_bins + 1),
             include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
  data.table(y = y[ord], exposure = exposure[ord], mu = mu[ord], bin = bin)[
    , .(Exposure = sum(exposure), Observed = sum(y) / sum(exposure), Predicted = sum(mu) / sum(exposure)), by = bin][order(bin)]
}
plot_lift <- function(mu, y, exposure, title) {
  dtl <- melt(decile_table(mu, y, exposure), id.vars = "bin",
              measure.vars = c("Observed", "Predicted"), variable.name = "Type", value.name = "Frequency")
  ggplot(dtl, aes(bin, Frequency, color = Type)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
    labs(title = title, x = "Predicted-risk decile (1 = lowest)", y = "Claim frequency") + theme_minimal()
}
print(plot_lift(mu_test_list[["GLM-B NB"]]$mu, test$NB_Claim, test$Exposure, "Lift -- GLM-B NB"))
print(plot_lift(mu_test_list[["CANN-NB"]]$mu, test$NB_Claim, test$Exposure, "Lift -- CANN-NB"))
```

# 7. Interpretation

The CANN is a diagnostic *on* the GLM, not a replacement for it: where a partial
dependence curve departs from the GLM's fitted effect, that's a missing spline, band,
or interaction you can put back into the GLM — yielding a transparent tariff informed
by the network rather than a black box in production.

We interpret a single representative fit (`nb_seed1`) rather than the seed-average,
since permutation importance and partial dependence need an actual fitted network to
re-predict from, not just its saved predictions.

```{r interp-setup}
interp_fit <- cann_fits[["nb_seed1"]]$fit
theta_interp <- 1 / exp(as.numeric(interp_fit$net$log_r))
predict_cann_from_raw <- function(fit, data) predict_cann(fit, mm(f_glmA, data), mlp_input(data), log(data$Exposure))
base_mu <- predict_cann_from_raw(interp_fit, test)
base_nll <- own_nll(base_mu, test$NB_Claim, "nb", theta_interp)
```

## 7.1 Permutation feature importance

Individually first, then the collinear telematics families **as a group** (shuffle
all columns in a family with the *same* row permutation) — individual permutation
understates importance under strong collinearity, since the model can partly
reconstruct a shuffled column's information from its correlated neighbours.

```{r interp-perm}
perm_importance <- function(vars, data = test, y = test$NB_Claim, theta, n_rep = 3, group = FALSE) {
  if (!group) {
    deltas <- sapply(vars, function(v) mean(sapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(i) {
      dperm <- copy(data); dperm[[v]] <- sample(dperm[[v]])
      own_nll(predict_cann_from_raw(interp_fit, dperm), y, "nb", theta) - base_nll
    })))
    data.table(feature = vars, delta_nll = deltas)
  } else {
    delta <- mean(sapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(i) {
      idx <- sample(nrow(data)); dperm <- copy(data)
      for (v in vars) dperm[[v]] <- dperm[[v]][idx]
      own_nll(predict_cann_from_raw(interp_fit, dperm), y, "nb", theta) - base_nll
    }))
    data.table(feature = paste(vars, collapse = " + "), delta_nll = delta)
  }
}

trad_vars <- c("Insured.age", "Car.age", "Credit.score", "Years.noclaims", "Annual.miles.drive",
               "Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use.grp")
indiv_importance <- perm_importance(c(trad_vars, telematics_glmB), theta = theta_interp)
setorder(indiv_importance, -delta_nll)
print(indiv_importance)
```

```{r interp-perm-group}
accel_family <- c("Accel.06miles","Accel.08miles","Accel.09miles","Accel.11miles","Accel.12miles","Accel.14miles")
brake_family <- c("Brake.06miles","Brake.08miles","Brake.09miles","Brake.11miles","Brake.12miles","Brake.14miles")
lturn_family <- c("Left.turn.intensity08","Left.turn.intensity09","Left.turn.intensity10","Left.turn.intensity11","Left.turn.intensity12")
rturn_family <- c("Right.turn.intensity08","Right.turn.intensity09","Right.turn.intensity10","Right.turn.intensity11","Right.turn.intensity12")
day_family   <- c("Pct.drive.mon","Pct.drive.tue","Pct.drive.wed","Pct.drive.thr","Pct.drive.fri","Pct.drive.sat","Pct.drive.sun")

group_importance <- rbindlist(list(
  perm_importance(accel_family, theta = theta_interp, group = TRUE),
  perm_importance(brake_family, theta = theta_interp, group = TRUE),
  perm_importance(lturn_family, theta = theta_interp, group = TRUE),
  perm_importance(rturn_family, theta = theta_interp, group = TRUE),
  perm_importance(day_family,   theta = theta_interp, group = TRUE)
))
setorder(group_importance, -delta_nll)
print(group_importance)

cat("\nGLM-B |z| ranking, for comparison -- where the CANN promotes a feature the GLM\n")
cat("under-weighted (or vice versa), that's a non-linearity or interaction worth reporting:\n")
print(as.data.table(summary(glmB_nb)$coefficients, keep.rownames = "term")[order(-abs(`z value`))])
```

## 7.2 Partial dependence: CANN vs GLM-B, on the same footing

Both curves are computed the same way (sweep the variable, average the predicted
frequency over the test set, holding everything else at its observed value), so the
gap between them is a direct picture of what the network added beyond the log-linear
fit.

```{r interp-pdp}
pdp_curve <- function(var, grid, predict_fn, data = test) {
  sapply(grid, function(v) { d <- copy(data); d[[var]] <- v; mean(predict_fn(d) / d$Exposure) })
}
plot_pdp <- function(var, grid) {
  cann_curve <- pdp_curve(var, grid, function(d) predict_cann_from_raw(interp_fit, d))
  glm_curve  <- pdp_curve(var, grid, function(d) predict(glmB_nb, d, type = "response"))
  dt <- data.table(x = rep(grid, 2), y = c(cann_curve, glm_curve),
                    Model = rep(c("CANN-NB", "GLM-B NB"), each = length(grid)))
  ggplot(dt, aes(x, y, color = Model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste("Partial dependence --", var), x = var, y = "Predicted frequency") + theme_minimal()
}
print(plot_pdp("Total.miles.driven", quantile(test$Total.miles.driven, seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 20))))
print(plot_pdp("Pct.drive.rush.pm",  quantile(test$Pct.drive.rush.pm,  seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 20))))
print(plot_pdp("Brake.06miles",      quantile(test$Brake.06miles,      seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 20))))
```

# 8. Scope boundary: why MVNB is not in this project

The paper's third specification, the Multivariate Negative Binomial, is its novel
contribution: a single Gamma frailty is drawn **per insured** and shared across all of
that insured's contract-years, so a driver with a bad frailty draw has elevated
claims in *every* year they're observed. That construction requires panel data —
repeated contracts for the same insured.

This public dataset is cross-sectional: one row per policy, no insured identifier, no
repeated contracts. With no within-insured dependence to model, the MVNB algebraically
reduces to the ordinary NB, and fitting it would add nothing but a fit on a form the
data cannot support. This is a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight — and
understanding *why* MVNB doesn't apply here is arguably a stronger demonstration of
the model than shoehorning it in would be.

Two further, smaller simplifications versus the paper: telematics here arrive
pre-aggregated per policy (the raw-trip-log preprocessing stage is skipped), and there
is no panel structure, so there is no credibility / experience-rating dimension to
model on top of the cross-sectional fit.

# 9. Conclusion

- Dispersion diagnostics justify Negative Binomial over Poisson (§4.2); the NB
  dispersion parameter α̂ falls substantially once telematics are added, meaning
  telematics explain part of the unobserved heterogeneity the traditional rating
  factors miss.
- GLM-B (hand-picked telematics) beats GLM-A (traditional only) out of sample — the
  paper's claim that telematics carry signal holds even through a log-linear lens.
- The headline comparison is `CANN-NB` vs `GLM-B NB` in the evaluation table (§6): does
  a *learned* telematics representation, warm-started from the GLM and free to use all
  ~38 raw telematics columns, beat a small, hand-picked, log-linear feature set.
- Permutation importance and partial dependence (§7) turn the CANN into a diagnostic
  on the GLM: where the network's fitted effect departs from the GLM's, that's a
  candidate spline, band or interaction to fold back into the transparent tariff.
- MVNB is out of scope by design (§8): this data has no panel structure for it to
  model.
